title: Advanced Winemaking Craft
description: Master top-level winemaking techniques: whole-cluster fermentation, oak barrel proportions, lees ageing, and more
lessons.0.title: The Art and Science of Whole-Cluster Fermentation
lessons.0.slides.0.title: The Art and Science of Whole-Cluster Fermentation
lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 1 - 18 min
lessons.0.slides.0.description: Understanding the debate and science behind whole-cluster (whole-bunch) fermentation
lessons.0.slides.1.title: Whole-Cluster Fermentation
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Whole-cluster fermentation means fermenting with the stems included rather than destemming. It is a Burgundy tradition that was largely abandoned in the mid-20th century (stems were seen as adding bitterness), but has resurged in recent decades as producers discovered that ripe stems add complexity, spice character, and a silkier tannin texture. Fully ripe stems are essential — unripe ones introduce herbaceous notes.
lessons.0.slides.2.title: 🍇 Effects of Whole-Cluster Fermentation
lessons.0.slides.2.points.0: Aromatics: adds spice, floral, and herbal notes (thyme, white pepper, carnation)
lessons.0.slides.2.points.1: Tannins: more tannin (+20–30%) but silkier texture
lessons.0.slides.2.points.2: Acidity: retains higher freshness (+0.5–1 g/L tartaric acid)
lessons.0.slides.2.points.3: Colour: lighter colour (intracellular fermentation reduces pigment extraction by 15–25%)
lessons.0.slides.2.points.4: Complexity: more layers and ageing potential (aromatic compounds +30–50%)
lessons.0.slides.2.points.5: Risk: unripe stems introduce herbaceous, green flavours (requires lignin content >30%)
lessons.0.slides.3.title: Historical Evolution of Whole-Cluster Technique
lessons.0.slides.4.title: 🍃 Stem Ripeness Assessment Criteria
lessons.0.slides.4.points.0: Colour: green (unripe) → brown (ripe) → dark brown (fully ripe)
lessons.0.slides.4.points.1: Texture: grassy and soft (unripe) → woody and firm (ripe)
lessons.0.slides.4.points.3: Tannin feel: bitter, astringent (unripe) → gentle, silky (ripe)
lessons.0.slides.4.points.4: Taste test: chew the end of a stem — any green flavour means it's not ready
lessons.0.slides.4.points.5: Harvest timing: stems usually fully ripen 3–7 days after the grapes
lessons.0.slides.5.title: 100% Whole-Cluster vs 100% Destemmed
lessons.0.slides.6.title: 🍇 Whole-Cluster Proportions at Top Estates
lessons.0.slides.6.content: A spectrum from 0% to 100% reflecting different winemaking philosophies. DRC insists on 100%; Henri Jayer's tradition was 0%; most estates use a flexible 30–70% approach.
lessons.0.slides.7.title: The Wisdom of Partial Whole-Cluster
lessons.0.slides.7.content: Most producers use partial whole-cluster (30–70%), adjusting by vintage and parcel. In warm years the proportion is reduced (to avoid excessive tannin); in cool years it's increased (to add complexity). Elegant parcels (Chambolle) suit higher whole-cluster, while powerful parcels (Gevrey) are better served with moderation.
lessons.0.slides.8.title: 💡 Key Points for Whole-Cluster Fermentation
lessons.0.slides.8.points.0: Stem ripeness matters more than grape ripeness
lessons.0.slides.8.points.1: Check stems: they should be brown and woody, not green
lessons.0.slides.8.points.2: Gentle extraction: avoid crushing stems and releasing bitterness
lessons.0.slides.8.points.4: Top producers adjust whole-cluster proportion year by year
lessons.0.slides.8.points.5: When tasting, look for spice, floral notes, silky tannins as markers
lessons.0.slides.9.title: 🧠 Whole-Cluster Fermentation Quiz
lessons.1.title: The Science of Oak Barrel Aging
lessons.1.slides.0.title: The Science of Oak Barrel Aging
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 2 - 17 min
lessons.1.slides.0.description: Exploring the science and art of oak barrel maturation
lessons.1.slides.1.title: Oak Barrels Are More Than Containers
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Oak barrels are not just vessels — they are part of the winemaking process itself. New oak imparts vanilla, toasted bread, smoke, and coconut aromas, while providing micro-oxygenation that softens tannins. But overuse can mask terroir expression. Top Burgundy producers precisely control new-oak percentages to achieve the perfect balance between wood and terroir.
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 🛢️ Key Parameters of Oak Barrels
lessons.1.slides.2.points.0: New-oak percentage: 0–100%; top Grand Crus typically 50–100% (DRC, Méo-Camuzet: 100%)
lessons.1.slides.2.points.1: Oak origin: French Allier (fine-grained), Tronçais (powerful), Vosges (gentle)
lessons.1.slides.2.points.2: Toast level: light (floral, vanilla), medium (vanilla, toasted bread), heavy (smoke, coffee)
lessons.1.slides.2.points.3: Barrel size: Burgundy 228 L vs Bordeaux 225 L (surface area affects oxygenation)
lessons.1.slides.2.points.4: Ageing duration: 12–24 months (Grand Crus longer; DRC 18–24 months)
lessons.1.slides.2.points.5: Old barrels: 2–5-year-old barrels provide ageing without wood flavour; cost only 10–15% of new
lessons.1.slides.3.title: Oak Barrel Production Process (3-year cycle)
lessons.1.slides.4.title: 🔥 Effect of Toast Level on Flavour
lessons.1.slides.4.points.0: Light Toast: temp <200 °C, 15–20 min → floral, vanilla, white pepper
lessons.1.slides.4.points.1: Medium Toast: temp 200–220 °C, 25–30 min → vanilla, toasted bread, caramelised sugar
lessons.1.slides.4.points.2: Medium+ Toast: temp 220–230 °C, 30–35 min → caramel, coffee, cocoa
lessons.1.slides.4.points.3: Heavy Toast: temp >230 °C, 35–45 min → smoke, char, grilled meat
lessons.1.slides.4.points.4: Burgundy preference: mainly medium to medium+; balances oak and terroir
lessons.1.slides.4.points.5: DRC custom: uses own Allier forest oak, made by cooper François Frères
lessons.1.slides.5.title: 🔥 Toast Level Comparison (Light vs Heavy)
lessons.1.slides.5.content: Toast level determines the aromatic style imparted by the barrel. Burgundy favours medium to medium+ (200–230 °C), which provides toasted bread and caramel aromas without overwhelming terroir expression.
lessons.1.slides.6.title: High New-Oak vs Low New-Oak
lessons.1.slides.7.title: 🛢️ New-Oak Percentages at Top Estates (Red vs White)
lessons.1.slides.7.content: Reds can tolerate 80–100% new oak; whites use only 20–40%. Tannin structure is the key difference. DRC/Méo reds use 100% new oak, but Coche-Dury whites use only 25%.
lessons.1.slides.8.title: White vs Red Wine Differences
lessons.1.slides.8.content: White wines are far more sensitive to new oak because they lack tannins for structure. Top white wine producers (e.g. Coche-Dury) use only 20–30% new oak, preventing wood from masking delicate minerality. Reds can handle higher proportions — DRC uses 100% new oak — but need 15–20 years to fully integrate it.
lessons.1.slides.9.title: 🌳 Oak Barrel Quality Differences
lessons.1.slides.9.points.1: Wood drying: natural air-drying 3+ years > kiln-drying
lessons.1.slides.9.points.2: Cooperage skill: premium coopers like François Frères command high prices
lessons.1.slides.9.points.3: Toast precision: temperature and duration carefully controlled
lessons.1.slides.9.points.4: DRC's own forest: ensures consistent oak quality
lessons.1.slides.9.points.5: Cost: one new French oak barrel ~€1,000–1,500
lessons.1.slides.10.title: 🧠 Oak Barrel Ageing Quiz
lessons.2.title: Lees Aging and Bâtonnage Techniques
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Lees Aging and Bâtonnage Techniques
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 - 15 min
lessons.2.slides.0.description: The science and art of lees ageing and stirring
lessons.2.slides.1.title: The Role of Lees
lessons.2.slides.1.content: Lees are the dead yeast cells that settle to the bottom of the barrel after fermentation. Sur lie (on-lees) ageing keeps the wine in contact with the lees; as the yeast cells break down, they release polysaccharides, amino acids, and fatty acids, giving the wine a rounder mouthfeel, bread-like aromas, and antioxidant protection. This is especially important for white wine.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: 🥖 Benefits of Lees Ageing
lessons.2.slides.2.points.1: Aromas: bread, butter, and nut notes (from autolysis products)
lessons.2.slides.2.points.2: Protection: antioxidant, preserving freshness (SO₂ use reduced 30–50%)
lessons.2.slides.2.points.3: Complexity: more layers and depth (amino acids and fatty acids released)
lessons.2.slides.2.points.4: Stability: reduces protein precipitation (yeast cell walls bind proteins)
lessons.2.slides.2.points.5: Integration: helps oak flavours meld with the wine (polysaccharides soften wood by 20–30%)
lessons.2.slides.3.title: 🧬 Biochemical Process of Lees Ageing
lessons.2.slides.3.points.0: Phase 1 (months 1–3): autolysis begins; cell walls rupture, releasing polysaccharides and amino acids
lessons.2.slides.3.points.1: Phase 2 (months 3–6): continued autolysis; fatty acids and growth hormones released, mouthfeel rounds out
lessons.2.slides.3.points.2: Phase 3 (months 6–12): deep autolysis; nucleic acids released, complexity increases
lessons.2.slides.3.points.3: Phase 4 (months 12–18): yeast fully decomposed; flavour compounds fully integrated with the wine
lessons.2.slides.3.points.4: Key figures: ~1 billion yeast cells per gram of lees; ~7–10 mg/L of compounds released
lessons.2.slides.3.points.5: Temperature: 12–14 °C constant; higher temperature accelerates autolysis but reduces finesse
lessons.2.slides.4.title: Bâtonnage Strategies Compared at Top White-Wine Estates
lessons.2.slides.5.title: Bâtonnage (Lees Stirring)
lessons.2.slides.5.content: Bâtonnage means using a stick to stir the lees settled at the barrel bottom, re-suspending them for greater contact with the wine. Traditionally done weekly for 6–12 months. Modern producers are more cautious — excessive bâtonnage reduces freshness and minerality. Coche-Dury stirs weekly for the first 6 months, then stops and lets the wine rest.
lessons.2.slides.6.title: Barrel Lees Profile and Bâtonnage Effect
lessons.2.slides.7.title: More Bâtonnage vs Less Bâtonnage
lessons.2.slides.8.title: ⚗️ Lees Ageing in Practice
lessons.2.slides.8.points.3: Monitoring: regular tasting to avoid over-development
lessons.2.slides.8.points.4: Red wines: also aged on lees but stirred less frequently
lessons.2.slides.8.points.5: Top producers: fine-tune based on vintage and individual barrel
lessons.2.slides.9.title: 🧠 Lees Management and Bâtonnage Quiz
lessons.3.title: Malolactic Fermentation and Acidity Management
lessons.3.slides.0.title: Malolactic Fermentation and Acidity Management
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 4 - 16 min
lessons.3.slides.0.description: Understanding MLF and how producers manage acidity under climate change
lessons.3.slides.1.title: Malolactic Fermentation (MLF)
lessons.3.slides.1.content: MLF is the secondary fermentation that follows alcoholic fermentation: lactic acid bacteria convert the sharp malic acid into gentle lactic acid, lowering total acidity and adding roundness. Nearly all Burgundy reds and most whites undergo MLF. But with warming temperatures, some producers are now experimenting with blocking or partially blocking MLF to retain acidity.
lessons.3.slides.2.title: 🧪 Effects of Malolactic Fermentation
lessons.3.slides.2.points.0: Acidity: total acidity reduced by ~2–4 g/L
lessons.3.slides.2.points.1: Mouthfeel: from sharp to soft and round
lessons.3.slides.2.points.2: Aromas: adds butter and nut notes
lessons.3.slides.2.points.4: Timing: usually occurs naturally in winter
lessons.3.slides.2.points.5: Control: temperature and bacterial strain affect outcome
lessons.3.slides.3.title: The Challenge of a Warming Climate
lessons.3.slides.3.content: In warm vintages since 2003, Burgundy grapes generally show lower acidity. Traditionally MLF was essential, but now some producers question this. In hot years (2018, 2019, 2022), certain estates have blocked MLF in whites to preserve acidity and freshness. This marks a significant shift in Burgundy's winemaking philosophy.
lessons.3.slides.4.title: Full MLF vs Partial/Blocked MLF
lessons.3.slides.5.title: 🌡️ Acidity Management Techniques
lessons.3.slides.5.points.0: Earlier harvest: retains higher acidity (the primary method)
lessons.3.slides.5.points.1: Blocking MLF: use SO₂ or cold temperatures to inhibit bacteria
lessons.3.slides.5.points.2: Partial MLF: allow some barrels to complete MLF then blend
lessons.3.slides.5.points.3: Tartaric acid addition: rarely used; damages terroir expression
lessons.3.slides.5.points.4: Canopy management: increase shade cover to preserve acidity
lessons.3.slides.5.points.5: Future trend: acidity management becoming an essential skill
lessons.3.slides.6.title: 🧠 Malolactic Fermentation Management Quiz
lessons.4.title: Maceration and Extraction Techniques
lessons.4.slides.0.title: Maceration and Extraction Techniques
lessons.4.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 5 - 15 min
lessons.4.slides.0.description: The art and science of skin contact and extraction in Burgundy red wine
lessons.4.slides.1.title: The Art of Maceration
lessons.4.slides.1.content: Maceration is the process of keeping grape juice in contact with skins and seeds to extract pigments, tannins, and aromatic compounds. Burgundy reds typically macerate for 15–30 days — far longer than the New World (7–14 days). This gives Burgundy reds their complex tannic structure and ageing potential, but requires a gentle approach to avoid over-extraction.
lessons.4.slides.2.title: 🍷 Key Phases of Maceration
lessons.4.slides.2.points.0: Cold soak (5–7 days): 5–10 °C; extracts aromatics and pigments only, not tannins (no alcohol to dissolve them)
lessons.4.slides.2.points.1: Alcoholic fermentation (7–10 days): 28–32 °C; main extraction period — pigments, tannins, and aromatics all extracted
lessons.4.slides.2.points.2: Post-fermentation maceration (3–14 days): 25–28 °C; extracts gentle tannins and integrates structure
lessons.4.slides.2.points.3: Total maceration: 15–30 days (top Grand Crus longer; DRC typically 25–35 days)
lessons.4.slides.2.points.4: Temperature control: never exceeds 33 °C — excess heat extracts bitter tannins
lessons.4.slides.2.points.5: Gentle extraction: avoid crushing seeds and releasing bitter seed tannins (6–8× more bitter)
lessons.4.slides.3.title: Red Wine Maceration Temperature Curve (typical 28-day cycle)
lessons.4.slides.4.title: Extraction Techniques at Top Estates Compared
lessons.4.slides.5.title: Pigeage vs Remontage
lessons.4.slides.5.content: Pigeage (punch-down) pushes the cap of skins floating on top back down into the wine, increasing extraction. Remontage (pump-over) pumps wine from the bottom and pours it over the cap. Burgundy traditionally prefers the gentler pigeage, considering pump-over too aggressive. DRC, Leroy, and other top estates insist on hand pigeage — labour-intensive but gentle and precise extraction.
lessons.4.slides.6.title: Gentle Extraction vs Aggressive Extraction
lessons.4.slides.7.title: 💡 The Wisdom of Extraction
lessons.4.slides.7.points.0: Variety character: Pinot Noir has thin skins — gentle extraction essential
lessons.4.slides.7.points.1: Vintage adjustment: reduce extraction in powerful years; increase in gentle years
lessons.4.slides.7.points.2: Parcel character: elegant parcels call for gentle technique
lessons.4.slides.7.points.3: Daily monitoring: taste daily to decide extraction level
lessons.4.slides.7.points.4: Seed ripeness: unripe seeds cause bitterness
lessons.4.slides.7.points.5: Goal: extract enough but not too much
lessons.4.slides.8.title: 🧠 Maceration and Extraction Quiz
lessons.5.title: Filtration, Fining, and Bottling
lessons.5.slides.0.title: Filtration, Fining, and Bottling
lessons.5.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 6 - 14 min
lessons.5.slides.0.description: The final steps in winemaking: filtration, fining, and bottling
lessons.5.slides.1.title: The Filtration Debate
lessons.5.slides.1.content: Filtration removes tiny particles and microorganisms from wine, improving stability and clarity — but may strip out some flavour compounds and texture. Top estates (DRC, Leroy) refuse to filter, believing it harms terroir expression. Yet excellent producers also use light filtration, arguing that moderate filtration does not affect quality.
lessons.5.slides.2.title: Unfiltered vs Filtered
lessons.5.slides.3.title: Fining
lessons.5.slides.3.content: Fining adds clarifying agents (egg white, bentonite, etc.) to adsorb suspended particles and cause them to settle. Burgundy traditionally uses fresh egg whites (3–6 per barrel) — gentle and flavour-safe. Modern estates also use bentonite and PVPP. Top estates tend not to fine, or fine only lightly, allowing time and gravity to settle the wine naturally.
lessons.5.slides.4.title: 🍾 Choosing the Right Bottling Moment
lessons.5.slides.4.points.0: Traditional timing: bottle after 18 months in oak
lessons.5.slides.4.points.1: Lunar calendar: biodynamic estates choose 'fruit days' or 'flower days'
lessons.5.slides.4.points.2: Delayed bottling: DRC bottles 6–12 months later than most
lessons.5.slides.4.points.3: Early bottling: preserves primary fruit (less common)
lessons.5.slides.4.points.4: Batch bottling: large estates bottling in batches may see bottle-to-bottle variation
lessons.5.slides.4.points.5: Estate bottling: 'Mis en bouteille au domaine' — a quality guarantee
lessons.5.slides.5.title: 💎 The Essence of Top-Level Winemaking
lessons.5.slides.5.points.1: Precise control: every parameter deeply considered
lessons.5.slides.5.points.2: Vintage adaptation: no fixed formula — adjust with the climate
lessons.5.slides.5.points.3: Patience: don't rush bottling — allow the wine to develop naturally
lessons.5.slides.5.points.4: Quality above all: cost is not a constraint at top estates
lessons.5.slides.5.points.5: Continuous learning: even century-old estates keep evolving
lessons.5.slides.6.title: 🧠 Filtration and Bottling Quiz
